repertoires.title: The Italian Game
repertoires.blurb: The oldest opening in chess. Quick development, and the bishop points straight at Black's weakest square.

repertoires.title: The Ruy Lopez
repertoires.blurb: The Spanish Game. World champions have leaned on it for 150 years — slow pressure rather than a quick punch.

repertoires.title: The Scotch Game
repertoires.blurb: Break the centre open on move three. Far less theory than the Ruy Lopez, and it leads to open, tactical play.

repertoires.title: Queen's Gambit Declined
repertoires.blurb: The classical way to play 1.d4. Not really a gambit — you almost always get the pawn back.

repertoires.title: The London System
repertoires.blurb: The same setup against almost anything Black plays. The lowest-theory way to start a serious 1.d4 repertoire.

repertoires.title: The English Opening
repertoires.blurb: Start on the flank and take the centre later. Flexible, positional, and far less theory than 1.e4.

repertoires.title: The Catalan
repertoires.blurb: A Queen's Gambit with the bishop on g2. Quiet, lasting pressure on the long diagonal.

repertoires.title: The King's Gambit
repertoires.blurb: Throw the f-pawn forward on move two. The romantic opening: open lines and a fast attack, with real risk to your own king.

repertoires.title: Sicilian: Najdorf
repertoires.blurb: The sharpest answer to 1.e4, and Fischer's and Kasparov's weapon of choice. You play for a win, not a draw.

repertoires.title: Sicilian: Accelerated Dragon
repertoires.blurb: A Sicilian with far less theory than the Najdorf. The bishop on g7 does the work.

repertoires.title: Sicilian: Dragon
repertoires.blurb: Fianchetto the bishop on the long diagonal and race White's attack. One of the sharpest main lines in chess.

repertoires.title: The French Defense
repertoires.blurb: Solid and strategic. You concede space early and spend the game undermining White's centre.

repertoires.title: The Caro-Kann
repertoires.blurb: As solid as the French, but the light-squared bishop gets out first. A favourite of players who hate bad positions.

repertoires.title: Alekhine's Defence
repertoires.blurb: Invite White's pawns forward, then attack them. Provocative and hypermodern, and most opponents know little theory against it.

repertoires.title: King's Indian Defence
repertoires.blurb: Hand White the centre, then blow it up. The sharpest way to play for a win with Black against 1.d4.

repertoires.title: Nimzo-Indian Defence
repertoires.blurb: Pin the knight, trade it for the bishop, and play against the damaged pawns. The most respected answer to 1.d4.

repertoires.title: Grünfeld Defence
repertoires.blurb: Let White build a huge centre, then take it apart. Hypermodern chess in its purest form.

repertoires.title: Semi-Slav Defence
repertoires.blurb: Rock solid, and it hides some of the sharpest theory in chess. Support d5 twice, then unleash ...c5 or ...b5.

repertoires.title: Modern Benoni
repertoires.blurb: Unbalanced from move three. A queenside pawn majority and the long diagonal, against White's big centre.
